metadata.title: Why Your Track Gets Turned Down
metadata.note: Audio-concept explainer: loudness normalisation. Through-line: making a track louder buys nothing, because the platform turns it back down — and the room you crushed to get there does not come back. Sibling to the MP3 reel: that one was what happens inside your file, this is what happens after you upload it. Seven beats: four purpose-built scenes (B01-B04), one library ClaudeWindow (B05), ClaudeComposerAsk opener (B00), ClaudeTitleOutro (B06). AUDIENCE NOTE (per Rohan, 2026-09-10): viewers are NOT audio professionals. No 'master', 'mix', 'dynamics', 'limiter' or 'compression' without a plain-language definition first. EVERY NUMBER MEASURED on this machine with ffmpeg's EBU R128 scanner — see MEASUREMENTS.txt. NAME PRONUNCIATION: narration_text spells the presenter phonetically as 'Row-Haan VeeJayKooMaar'; all ON-SCREEN text keeps 'Rohan Vijaykumar'. OUTRO: uses HaiTitleOutro, not ClaudeTitleOutro — OUTRO-LOCK.md scopes ClaudeTitleOutro to claude-liam/@NikBearBrown reels ONLY and it now hardcodes that handle and drops the subline. Caught by visual QC on 2026-09-10. APPLY BEAT: uses HaiApplyCard, not ClaudeWindow — Gate V measured ClaudeWindow at 21% safe-area fill against a 55% floor (MAJOR underfill, blocks final).

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Row-Haan, for Humanitarians AI. You finish a track, and it sounds quieter than everything else in the playlist. So you turn it up. Here's the problem: the platform is going to turn it back down again, to exactly the level everyone else is at. So what did turning it up actually get you?

props.segment: Why Your Track Gets Turned Down
props.command: My track sounds quieter than other songs, so I pushed it louder. Spotify turned it back down. What did I actually gain?
output: nothing — the gain is erased on playback
loud is not the same thing as peak
what you crushed does not come back

beats.narration_text: Here are two versions of the same piece of music, both made on this machine. The top one I left alone. The bottom one I squeezed — I pulled the quiet moments up until they nearly matched the loud ones. Now look at the tallest point of each. Half a decibel apart. But the bottom one sounds nearly nine times louder.

props.title: Same Tallest Point. Very Different Loudness.
props.sparkLine: The tallest point tells you almost nothing.
props.footnote: Measured here with ffmpeg's EBU R128 scanner on a 30-second test signal I built for this.

beats.narration_text: That's because two different things are being measured. The tallest point is one instant: the single loudest sample in the track. Loudness is an average over time, weighted the way your ear hears. A track can spike once and sit quiet for the rest of the song. Your ear notices the quiet. A peak meter doesn't.

props.title: One Instant, or the Whole Song
props.peakSub: one instant — the single loudest sample
props.loudSub: the average over time, weighted like your ear
props.sparkLine: Your ear hears the whole song. A peak meter hears one moment.
props.footnote: The loudness scale is called LUFS. You do not need the acronym — you need to know it is an average, not a spike.

beats.narration_text: Here's what the platform does. It measures your loudness and turns the whole track up or down to match a target, around minus fourteen. My untouched version needed to come up one decibel. My squeezed version came down seven and a half. Every bit of loudness I fought for was removed before anyone heard it.

props.title: The Platform Puts Everyone on the Same Level
props.verdict: Both arrive at the same loudness.
props.footnote: Targets differ between platforms and change over time. The behaviour does not: loud tracks get turned down.
props.sparkLine: You cannot win a race the platform resets.

beats.narration_text: And here's the cost. To get loud, I pulled the quiet parts up to meet the loud ones. That gap went from twelve down to less than one. The loudness came back off. The gap did not. I applied the same volume change to both files: the loudness numbers moved, the gap didn't budge.

props.title: The Loudness Comes Back Off. The Room Does Not.
props.rangeLabel: GAP BETWEEN THE QUIETEST AND LOUDEST MOMENTS
props.proofLabel: SAME VOLUME CHANGE APPLIED TO BOTH
props.sparkLine: Loudness is borrowed. The gap is spent.
props.footnote: Measured: EBU R128 loudness range, before and after an identical gain change on both files.

beats.narration_text: So what do you do? Stop chasing loud. Leave the loudest moment about a decibel under the ceiling, and stop. Keep the gap between your quiet and loud parts — it's the only thing the platform won't touch. And if it still sounds small at the same volume, fix the arrangement.

props.title: What to Do Instead
props.lede: Stop chasing loud. The platform has already decided that number.
steps: Leave the loudest moment about a decibel under the ceiling, and stop there.
Keep the gap between your quiet and loud parts — it is the only thing the platform will not touch.
Do not squeeze to compete on volume. That competition was cancelled.
If it still sounds small at the same volume, fix the arrangement, not the level.
props.sparkLine: The only thing the platform will not take back is the gap.

beats.narration_text: Loud is temporary — the platform decides that. The gap between quiet and loud is yours, and you spend it once. I'm Row-Haan VeeJayKooMaar, for Humanitarians AI.
